name: City Council Regular Meeting - 7:00 PM
agenda_text:
CITY COUNCIL OF MONTEREY PARK
AND THE CITY COUNCIL ACTING ON BEHALF OF THE SUCCESSOR AGENCY OF THE FORMER
  REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY
  AGENDA

  REGULAR MEETING
  Monterey Park City Hall Council Chambers
  320 W. Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754

  Wednesday
  February 20, 2019
  7:00 p.m.

  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent services
  to enhance the quality of life for our entire community.

Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at
320 West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s
website at www.montereypark.ca.gov.
PUBLIC COMMENTS ON AGENDA ITEMS
You may speak up to 5 minutes on Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with
another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers.
Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting
please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359 for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a
meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair accessible.
This Agenda includes items considered by the City Council acting on behalf of the Successor Agency
of the former Monterey Park Redevelopment Agency which dissolved February 1, 2012. Successor
Agency matters will include the notation of “SA” next to the Agenda Item Number.

CALL TO ORDER  Mayor at
FLAG SALUTE  The Monterey Park Police Explorers
ROLL CALL  Peter Chan, Mitchell Ing, Stephen Lam, Hans Liang, Teresa Real Sebastian

AGENDA ADDITIONS, DELETIONS, CHANGES AND ADOPTIONS

PUBLIC COMMUNICATIONS. While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City
Council to take action on any item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments
after Public Communications is closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City
Council's subject-matter jurisdiction, comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public
comment on a specific Agenda item at this time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the
time the Agenda Item is considered.

ORAL AND WRITTEN COMMUNICATIONS

[1.]  PRESENTATION - None.

  Page 1 of 579
   Monterey Park City Council and Successor Agency Agenda, February 20, 2019 - Page 2

[2.]  OLD BUSINESS – None.

[3.]  CONSENT CALENDAR ITEMS NOS. 3A-3G

3-A.  WARRANT REGISTER FOR SUCCESSOR AGENCY TO THE FORMER COMMUNITY
  REDEVELOPMENT AGENCY OF FEBRUARY 20, 2019
  It is recommended that the City Council (acting on behalf of the Successor Agency):
  (1)  Approve payment of warrants and adopt a Resolution of the Successor Agency to the
  former Monterey Park Redevelopment Agency allowing certain claims and demands per
  warrant register dated February 20, 2019 totaling $458.00 and specifying the funds out of
  which the same are to be paid; and
  (2)  Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-B.  SUCCESSOR AGENCY MONTHLY INVESTMENT REPORT – JANUARY 2019
  It is recommended that the City Council (acting on behalf of the Successor Agency):
  (1)  Receive and file the Monthly Investment Report; and
  (2)  Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-C.  WARRANT REGISTER FOR THE CITY OF MONTEREY PARK OF FEBRUARY 20, 2019
  It is recommended that the City Council:
  (1)  Approve payment of warrants and adopt a Resolution allowing certain claims and
  demands per Warrant Register dated February 20, 2019 totaling $588,141.87 specifying
  the funds out of which the same are to be paid; and
  (2)  Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-D.  MONTHLY INVESTMENT REPORT – JANUARY 2019
  It is recommended that the City Council:
  (1)  Receive and file the monthly investment report; and
  (2)  Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-E.  MINUTES
  It is recommended that the City Council (acting on behalf of the Successor Agency):
  (1)  Approve the minutes from the special and regular meeting of January 16, 2019; and
  (2)  Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

  Page 2 of 579
   Monterey Park City Council and Successor Agency Agenda, February 20, 2019 - Page 3

3-F.  SECOND READING AND ADOPTION: AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE MONTEREY
  PARK MUNICIPAL CODE (“MPMC”) BY ENACTING VARIOUS PROVISIONS TO ENFORCE
  THE CITY-WIDE PROHIBITION UPON CANNABIS ACTIVITIES NOT OTHERWISE
  ALLOWED BY CALIFORNIA LAW
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1)  Waive the second reading and adopt the proposed ordinance; and
  (2)  Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

3-G.  SECOND READING AND ADOPTION:  AN ORDINANCE REGULATING SIDEWALK
  VENDING IN ACCORDANCE WITH GOVERNMENT CODE §§ 51036, ET SEQ.
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1)  Waive the second reading and adopt the proposed ordinance; and
  (2)  Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

[4.]  PUBLIC HEARING

4-A.  PUBLIC HEARING TO RECEIVE INPUT FROM THE COMMUNITY REGARDING THE
  CREATION OF A CITY COUNCIL DISTRICT-BASED ELECTORAL SYSTEM PURSUANT TO
  ELECTIONS CODE §10010

  It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  (1)  Receiving a report regarding the districting process and permissible criteria to be
  considered to create district boundaries;
  (2)  Conduct a Public Hearing to receive public testimony on the composition of districts for a
  district-based electoral system pursuant to Elections Code § 10010;
  (3)  Provide direction to the City’s demographer regarding the composition of districts for a
  district-based electoral system pursuant to Elections Code § 10010; and
  (4)  Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

4-B.  ANNUAL WEED ABATEMENT PROTEST HEARING
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1)  Open public hearing, receive public comment, close the public hearing;
  (2)  Any complaints received from parcel owners will be referred to L.A. County for follow-up
  and City staff will monitor the status of any complaints; and
  (3)  Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

  Page 3 of 579
   Monterey Park City Council and Successor Agency Agenda, February 20, 2019 - Page 4

[5.]  NEW BUSINESS

5-A.  PROFESSIONAL SERVICES AGREEMENT FOR THE GENERAL PLAN UPDATE PROJECT
  AND THE AUTHORIZATION OF ADDITIONAL FUNDING FOR THE PROJECT
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1)  Authorizing the City Manager to execute a professional services agreement with MIG, Inc.
  to provide professional services related to the General Plan update project;
  (2)  Authorize an additional $349,607 to cover the cost of the General Plan update project; and
  (3)  Alternatively, discuss and take other action related to this item.

5-B.  APPOINT MEMBERS TO THE GENERAL PLAN ADVISORY COMMITTEE
  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1)  Appointing members to the General Plan Advisory Committee;
  (2)  Appointing five alternates: and
  (3)  Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

[6.]  [7.]
  COUNCIL COMMUNICATIONS AND MAYOR/COUNCIL AND AGENCY MATTERS

[7.]  CLOSED SESSION (IF REQUIRED; CITY ATTORNEY TO ANNOUNCE)

ADJOURN

SECTION 1: The C ity Council finds and determines as follows

  A.  Article Xl, S 7 of the California Constitution empowers the City to enact
  and enforce ordinances regulating conditions that may be public
  nuisances or health hazards, or that promote social, economic, or
  aesthetic considerations.

  B.  Government Code S 38771 permits general law cities to identify public
  nuisances by ordinance.

  c.  Code of Civil Procedure S 731 permits civil actions to be brought in the
  name of the people of the state of California to abate public nuisances.

  D  Government Code S 53069.4 authorizes the City Council to subject
  violations of the MPMC to administrative fines or penalties. To impose
  such penalties, the Government Code generally requires that the City
  provide a reasonable time to remedy a violation before the fines can be
  imposed; especially where the violation pertains to building, plumbing,
  electrical or other similar issues (collectively, "uniform code violations").

  E.  Effective January 1,2019, the City may also enact an ordinance
  providing for the immediate imposition of administrative fines or
  penalties for uniform code violations where these violations resulted
  from illegal cannabis cultivation.

  F  The Federal Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. S 801, et seq.,
  classifies cannabis as a Schedule 1 Drug, which is defined as a drug
  or other substance that has a high potential for abuse, that has no
  currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States, and
  that has not been accepted as safe for use under medical supervision.
  The Federal Controlled Substances Act makes it unlawful under
  federal law for any person to cultivate, manufacture, distribute or
  dispense, or possess with intent to manufacture, distribute or dispense,
  cannabis.

  G.  The penalties for violating federal law include fines between $10,000
  and $50,000 (21 U.S.C. S 841) for first time offenders. California law

  has similar provisions (see, e.9., Health and Safety Code SS 11372
  and 1 1379.6).

  H  As of the effective date of this Ordinance, the City has not authorized
  any commercial cannabis activity within its jurisdiction. To the contrary,
  Monterey Park Municipal Code ('MPMC") S 21.46.020 explicitly
  prohibits such activity.

  The City's ability to abate public nuisances through its police powers is
  well-established (see, e.9., Civil Code SS 3479, 3480; People ex rel.
  Gallo v. Acuna (1997) 14 Cal.4th 1090; People v. Greene (1968) 264
  Cal.App.2d774).

  J  City's ability to recover its nuisance abatement costs through local
  regulations, including, without limitation, reasonable attorney's fees, is
  also recognized (see City of Santa Paula v. Narula (2003) 114
  Cal.App.4th 485, reh'q. den.2004; City of Flagstaff v. Atchison,
  Topeka and Santa Fe Railway Co. (9th Cir. 1983) 719 F.2d 322).

  K.  A statewide initiative entitled the "Control, Regulate and Tax Adult Use
  of Marijuana Act" ('AUMA")was approved by voters on the November
  2016 ballot. AUMA does not, and cannot, affect federal regulations as
  to cannabis or its derivatives.

  L  AUMA expressly preserves local control over the regulation of
  cannabis-related businesses and cannabis-related land uses
  (Business & Professions Code S 26200, ef seg.).

  M  ln City of Riverside v. lnland Empire Patients Health and Wellness
  Center, lnc. (2013) 56 Cal.4th 729,lhe California Supreme Court held
  that "[n]othing in the CUA or the MMP expressly or impliedly limits the
  inherent authori$ of a localjurisdiction, by its own ordinances, to
  regulate the use of its land. . . ." Additionally, in Maralv. City of Live
  Oak (2O13) 221 Cal.App.4th 975, the Court of Appeal held that "there
  is no right - and certainly no constitutional right - to cultivate medical
  marijuana. . . . ." The Court in Maral affirmed the ability of a local
  governmental entig to prohibit the cultivation of cannabis under its land
  use authority.

  protect citizens and their property from conditions that threaten public
  health, safety, and welfare including, without limitation, matters that

  such penalties, the Government Code generally requires that the City
  provide a reasonable time to remedy a violation before the fines can be
  imposed; especially where the violation pertains to building, plumbing,
  electrical or other similar issues (collectively, "uniform code violations").

  E  Effective January 1,2019, the City may also enact an ordinance
  providing for the immediate imposition of administrative fines or

  that has not been accepted as safe for use under medical supervision.
  The Federal Controlled Substances Act makes it unlawful under
  federal law for any person to cultÍvate, manufacture, distribute or
  dispense, or possess with intent to manufacture, distribute or dispense,

  THE CITY COUNCIL DOES ORDAIN AS FOLLOWS:

  SECTION 1. The City Councilfinds and determines as follows:

  A  Government Code SS 51036, ef seg, became etfective on January 1,2019
  and acts to, among other things, decriminalize sidewalk vending.

  B  Amendments to the MPMC implemented by this Ordinance are necessary
  to create a Sidewalk Vending Program which will provide licensing
  regulations of street vendors in Monterey Park and limit penalties to a
  specified schedule of fines.

  SECTION 2. Factual Findings and Conclusions. The City Council finds that the
following facts exist and makes the following conclusions:

  A  Based upon documentary information and law enforcement reporting, many
  sidewalk vendors in the City engage in public nuisances including, without
  limitation: operating at or near parking lots and driveways (see California
  Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices and California Department of
  Transportation 2014 Highway Design Manual), in addition to urinating and
  defecating in public; vandalism; littering and unlawful depositing of refuse;
  and operating in a manner interfering with the normalflow of pedestrian and
  vehicle traffic (see compilation of offenses from 2008 to the present related
  to vendors, prepared by the Monterey Park Police Department, attached as
  "Exhibit A"). Additionally, the City has also received reports regarding
  sidewalk vendors violating public health regulations governing food service.

  B  Street food vending has become an important public health issue and a
  great concern due to widespread food borne diseases caused, in part, by
  food vendors who lack an adequate understanding of basic food safety and
  food-handling requirements. Major sources contributing to microbial
  contamination are the place of preparation, utensils for cooking and serving,
  raw materials, time and temperature of cooked foods and the personal
  hygiene of vendors (see Food & Drug Administration Employee Health &
  Personal  Hygiene  Handbook  at
  https://www.fda.gov/downloads/Food/GuidanceRegulation/RetailFoodProt
  ection/l nd ustryand Regu lato ryAssistan ceandTrai n i ng Resou rces/UCM 1 945
  75.pdf. Accessed December 17, 2018.);

  c  Obesity, especially among children and adolescents, is a critical issue. A
  policy restricting the proliferation of unhealthy food sources near school
  campuses and promoting the sale of healthier food near schools may help
  address this epidemic locally (see David C. Sloane, et al., "A Step Toward
  a Healthier South Los Angeles: lmproving Student Food Options Through
  Healthy Sidewalk Vendor Legalization." Cityscape: A Journal of Policy
  Development and Research, Volume 18, no. 1,2016 U.S. Department of
  Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and

  healthy-street-vendor-legalization/. Accessed December 17, 20 1 8); and

D  There is a need to regulate the sale of food and merchandise in the public
  right-of-way to ensure that vendors prepare food safely, and according to
  the requirements of the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health;
  to prevent unsanitary conditions; to ensure trash and debris are removed
  by vendors; and to safeguard pedestrian movement on the sidewalk.

  TO:  Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
  FROtbt:  Natalie C. Karpeles, Deputy City Attorney
  SUBJECT:  First reading and adoption of an Ordinance regulating sidewalk vending
  in accordance with Government Code SS 51036, ef seq.

REGOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  (1) Waiving first reading and introducing Ordinance  No._
  regulating sidewalk
  vending in accordance with Government Code SS 51036, ef seq; or
  (2) Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUIIIMARY:

Government Code SS 51036, ef seg. became effective on January 1,2019. Among other
things, the new law decriminalizes sidewalk vending. Staff recommends that the City
Council amend the MPMC to comply with the new law by adopting regulations governing
sidewalk vending.

BACKGROUND & DISCUSSION:

L  Historv

The City first adopted its street vendor regulations in 1971. Ordinance No. 2067 was
subsequently adopted on August 19, 2009 and amended the MPMC to generally prohibit
food vendor carts in the public right-of-way. From 2008 to the present, the Monterey Park
Police Department reported the following violations related to street vending: urinating
and defecating in public; vandalism; littering and unlawful depositing of refuse; and
operating in a manner interfering with the normal flow of pedestrian and vehicle traffic.
Attachment 1 is a compilation of offenses from 2008 to the present related to vendors,
prepared by the Monterey Park Police Department.

l¡.  Government Code S8 51036, ef seq.1

Government Code SS 51036, ef seg. decriminalize sidewalk vending and establish
various requirements for local regulation of sidewalk vendors.2 Should the CiÇ decide to
create a permitting program to regulate sidewalk vendors under Government Code $$
51036, ef seq., its provisions must substantially comply with the requirements outlined

  See Senate B¡ll 946, included as Attachment 2.
2 These sections do not impact the City's regulation  of food trucks and charitable solicitations, nor do they
impact the State's Retail Food Code.

therein and may only implement restrictions that are objectively related to health, safeÇ
or welfare concerns.3

lll.  Proposed Amendments

The City's vending regulations are currently dispersed among multiple chapters and
sections; the first goal of the draft ordinance is to create one chapter (Chapter 5.68) to
regulate sidewalk vending in the City. Accordingly, the City's previous regulations
regarding vendors or vending were consolidated into Chapter 5.68. For example, the
language ¡n SS 9.81.010 and P.A4l10 was incorporated into Chapter 5.68 (see, e.9., SS
5.68.050(P), 5.68.030 and 5.68.050 of the new ordinance).

ln addition to consolidation, staff identified the following health, safety and welfare
concerns related to sidewalk vending:

  o Vendors operating at or near parkíng lots and driveways (which creates a safety
  hazard for children and which also obstructs adequate sightlines for drivers);
  o Vendors urinating or defecating in public;
  o Vendors vandalizing private and public property;
  r Vendors liftering;
  ¡ Vendors operating in a manner interfering with the normalflow of pedestrian and
  vehicle traffic; and
  .  Vendors violating public health regulations governing food service.

The following additional requirements (includíng in MPMC S 5.68.050 of the draft
ordinance) are related to objective health, safety or welfare concerns:

  r Require that vendors obtain a vending license and permit from the City, and that
  they provide identifying information on the applications;
  . Require that vendors provide liability insurance;
  . Require that vendors obtain a permit for any ancillary items that will be placed in
  the public right-of-way;
  . Require that vendors provide proof of either a Food Handler Card or Certified Food
  Protection Manager certificate for themselves and the conveyance they will be
  vending from;
  . Require stationary vendors to provide trash receptacles and recycling containers
  to eliminate littering;
  . Require stationary vendors, who are present in one location for longer than one
  hour, to operate within 200 feet of an approved and readily available toilet and
  handwashing faciliÇ;
  o Prohibit vendors from offering junk food within 500 feet of any K-12 school between
  the hours of 6:00 am and 6:00 pm; and
  o Prohibit vending within designated distances from building entrances, parking lots,
  driveway aprons, intersections and emergency infrastructure (e.9., fire hydrants,
  red curbs).

lV.  Other Concerns

The MPMC currently includes regulations governing charitable and religious solicitations
- and requires persons engaging in charitable and religious solicitations to obtain a permit
from the City Manager. These regulations were adopted in 1966 and have not
substantially changed.

h 2A02, the United States Supreme Court held that regulation of noncommercial
solicitation may violate the First Amendment.a lndeed, the Supreme Court determined
that collecting funds for charitable, political or religious purposes involves a variety of
speech interests and is therefore protected by the First Amendment.s Accordingly, the
City may only regulate charitable street vending where its regulations are content-neutral,
are narrowly tailored to achieve a significant government interest, and allow ample
alternative channels of communication.6

Staff recommends omittíng specific reference to "noncommercial" solicitations and
allowing this conduct to be regulated pursuant to state law - as recommended in the
proposed ordinance (alternatively, the City Council may enact an ordinance which
provides for disclosure of information relating to solicitations or sales for charitable
purposes substantially similar to the disclosure requirements of state law).

  LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST

  SB 946, Lara. Sidewalk vendors,

  Existing law authoriees a local authority, by ordinance or resolution, to adopt requ¡rements for the public safety
  regulating any type of vending and the time. place, and manner of vending from a vehicle upon a street.

  This bill would prohibit a local authority, as deflned, from regulating sidewalk vendors, except in accordance with
  the provisions of the b¡ll. The bill would provide that a local authority is not required to adopt a new program to
  regulate sidewalk vendors if the local authority has established an existing program that substantially compl¡es
  with the provisions of the bill. The b¡ll would apply these provisions to a chartered or general law city, county, or
  city and county.

  The bill would requ¡re a local author¡ty that elects to adopt a sidewalk vending program to, among other things,
  not requ¡re a sidewalk vendor to operate within specific parts of the public right-of-wa¡ except when that
  restrict¡on is directly related to objective health, safet¡ or welfare concerns, and not restríct sidewalk vendors to
  operate only in a designated neighborhood or area, except as specified. The bill would authorize a local authority
  to, by ordinance or resolution, adopt additional requirements regulating the time, place, and manner of sidewalk
  vending, as specified, if the requirements are directly related to objective health, safety, or welfare concerns.
  The b¡ll would also authorize a local authority to proh¡bit sidewalk vendors in areas located within the immediate
  vicinity of a perm¡tted certified farmers' market and a permitted swap meetf as specified. and to restrict or
  prohibit sidewalk vendors within the immediate vic¡nity of an area designated for a temporary special permit

  SECTION l. The City Council finds and determines as follows:

  A.  Government Code SS 51036, ef seq. became effective on January 1,2019
  and acts to, among other things, decriminalize sidewalk vending.

  B.  Amendments to the MPMC implemented by this Ordinance are necessary
  to create a Sidewalk Vending Program which will provide licensing
  regulations of street vendors in Monterey Park and limit penalties to a
  specified schedule of fines.

  SECTION 2. Factual Findings and Conclusr'ons. The City Council finds that the
following facts exist and makes the following conclusions:

  A.  Based upon documentary information and law enforcement reporting, many
  sidewalk vendors in the City engage in public nuisances including, without
  limitation: operating at or near parking lots and driveways (see California
  Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices and California Department of
  Transportation 2014 Highway Design Manual), in addition to urinating and
  defecating in public; vandalism; littering and unlawful depositing of refuse;
  and operating in a manner interfering with the normalflow of pedestrian and
  vehicle traffic (see compilation of offenses from 2008 to the present related
  to vendors, prepared by the Monterey Park Police Department, attached as
  "Exhibit A"). Additionally, the City has also received reports regarding
  sidewalk vendors violating public health regulations governing food service.

  B.  Street food vending has become an important public health issue and a
  great concern due to widespread food borne diseases caused, in part, by
  food vendors who lack an adequate understanding of basic food safety and
  food-handling requirements. Major sources contributing to microbial
  contamination are the place of preparation, utensils for cooking and serving,
  raw materials, time and ternperature of cooked foods and the personal
  hygiene of vendors (see Food & Drug Administration Employee Health &
  Personal  Hygiene  Handbook  at

RECOMMENDATION:

  It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  (1) Receiving a report regarding the districting process and permissible criteria
  to be considered to create district boundaries;
  (2) Conduct a Public Hearing to receive public testimony on the composition of
  districts for a district-based electoral system pursuant to Elections Code $
  1 001 0;

  (3) Provide direction to the City's demographer regarding the composition of
  districts for a district-based electoral system pursuant to Elections Code $
  10010; and
  (4) Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

On November 7,2018, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 12043 declaring its
intent to transition from at-large to district-based elections for City Council commencing
with the General Municipal Election in March 2020. Elections Code S 10010 requires
that the City conduct four public hearings to receive community input on district
boundaries and maps for the formation of City Council districts.

On December 19,2018, the City Council conducted the second of four Public Hearings.
Community input regarding the composition of district boundaries is summarized in
Attachment 1.

Based on public input, the City Council's direction, and other legally required criteria, the
City's Demographer evaluated and submitted the proposed draft maps for public review
and comments. lt is recommended that the City Council give direction regarding which
final map product, with any necessary modifications, the City Council would like to
consider at the March 6th City Council Meeting.

BACKGROUND

Since November 7th, the City engaged in outreach efforts to inform the public about
district elections and the process associated with their formation. A webpage
(www.MontereyPark.ca.gov/DistrictElections) was uploaded to provide information
about district elections, including opportunities for when and how the public can be
engaged (translations available). The official notice of Public Hearings was translated
and published in the Monterey Park Press (English), La Opinión (Spanish), World
Journal (Chinese), and Saigon Times (Vietnamese). ln addition, a press release in
multiple languages was sent via email to local media and subscribers, and an article
was placed in the December 2018 and the February 2019 editions of the Monterey Park
Cascade which was mailed to every residence in the City.

At the December 19, 2018 council meeting, the City Council directed staff to conduct
additional outreach efforts to engage the community in the formation of city council
districts. On the week of Jan. 14, 2019, a postcard, in multiple languages, providing
notice of the formation of district based electoral system was mailed to each household
in the City. The announcement was also emailed to Cíty's Commissions and Board
members. Additional, public participation kits were made available throughout city hall
and an instructional video on how to use the participation tools was uploaded to the
webpage as well. Persons calling for more information and request for the kit were
mailed a public participation kit.

Leading up to the third public hearing, the City Clerk's office received multiple proposed
draft maps. These maps were evaluated by the City's Demographer and are confirmed
that they have met the standards established under the California Voting Right Act
(CVRA) and Federal Voting Rights Act (FVRA). Attachment 2 contains the proposed
maps for review and public comments.

Elections Code S 10010 requires that modifications to the boundary maps be
republished for public review at least seven days before City Council consideration. lt is
recommended that the City Council give direction regarding which final map product,
with any necessary modifications, the City Council would like to consider at the March 6,
2019 council meeting.

Next Steps

At the March 6,2019 City Council Meeting, the City Council will conduct a 4th Public
Hearing to adopt a preferred district map and to introduce an ordinance to transition to a
district-based electoral system. The ordinance would take effect 30 days after its
adoption and will govern the 2020 general municipal elections.

property owners.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

The County of Los Angeles Department of Agriculture Commissioner and Weights and
Measures Weed Abatement Division submitted to the City of Monterey Park the annual
Weed Abatement Declaration List and Resolution to be approved and adopted by the
City Council on February 6, 2019. This action declares a list of parcels to be potentially
hazardous to fire and thereby deemed public nuisances.

BACKGROUND:

ln 1992, the City of Monterey Park entered into a contract with County of Los Angeles
Department of Agriculture Commissioner and Weights and Measures to provide weed
abatement services to the City. At that time, both the Fire and Community Development
Departments worked in unison to address and abate weeds in the community.
Subsequent to reviewing the County's proposal, the City determined that the County
could better provide the weed abatement services currently handled by the City thereby
realizing a significant savings in staff time and financial resources. Moreover,
contracting with the County would also free up Fire and Code Enforcement staff
allowing time to focus on other important issues in the community.

WEED ABATEMENT PROCESS:

The Weed Abatement cycle begins with the compilation of the Weed Abatement
Declaration List ("Declaration List"). The Declaration List is a list of parcels in Monterey
Park which have been identified by inspection, to contain or have the potential to
contain weeds or brush sufficient to be considered a public nuisance. As required by the

year and sent the list to the City of Monterey Park for review. Based on direction from
the City Council during last year's weed abatement process, the Community Services
Director and Senior Code Enforcement Officer reviewed the declaration list and
conducted field inspections to verify whether parcels should be included on the
Declaration List. Based on staffs evaluation, parcels have either been removed or

The County along with the assistance from the City of Monterey Park identified and
listed a total of 1,571 improved and unimproved parcels on the Weed Abatement
Declaration List for this year. This is an increase of 107 parcels from last year. Note that
most of the parcels on the Declaration List will show up annually. This is because these
parcels are located in hillside areas of the City where the risk of fire is much greater.
The annual weed abatement process is a way to remind property owners of their
responsibility to maintain their slopes thereby minimizing fire hazards in the hillside
areas of the community.
The County mailed notices on or about February 1,2019 to the recorded owner of each
parcel included on the Declaration List declaring that their parcel is an existing, future or
"potential" hazard. The County advised that it considers a parcel a future or "potential"
hazard if the parcel is not completely landscaped or irrigated and there is a potential for
weed growth. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors established an inspection
fee of $42.37, an increase from last year's fee by $3.93, which is assessed against all
properties on the Declaration List whether cleared by the property owners or not.
Parcel owners who received notices from the County may challenge their inclusion on
the list. Parcel owners may request that the Council to remove their parcels from the list
if they feel that the County erred by including their parcel on the Declaration List.

The County advised the City that if parcel owners want their parcel to be removed from
the Declaration List, the County will conduct a re-inspection of the parcel to determine if
an error was made. After reinspecting the parcel, the County will advise the City of its
findings.

The County advised that this year's Declaration List includes both parcels that continue
to lack landscaping/irrigation and new parcels due resulting from complaints submitted
by residents, new inspections, and field surveys by County inspectors.

  SUBJECT:  Professional Services Agreement for the General Plan update project

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Authorizing the City Manager to execute a professional services agreement with
  MlG, lnc. to provide professional services related to the General Plan update
  project;
  2. Authorize an additional $349,607 to cover the cost of the General Plan update
  project; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

As part of the FY 201812019 annual budget, the City Council authorized funding to
Community and Economic Development Department to prepare an update to the City's
General Plan. The existing General Plan was approved by the City Council in 2001 for a
planning period of 20 years. Since the useful life of the current General Plan is coming
up on the 20 year mark, it is time to reevaluate the existing long range land use policies
in the 2001 General Plan.

Staff prepared a draft Request for Proposal (RFP) for circulation to professional
planning firms seeking their interest in assisting the City staff in the preparation of a
General Plan update. However, due to the significance of the General Plan and its land
use policies that guide long-term growth in the community, staff felt it was in the best
interest of the project to allow the City Council the ability to review and comment on the
draft RFP. The intent was to seek Council comments creating a more comprehensive
RFP before the document is circulated to interested professional planning firms.

At the December 5, 2018 meeting, the City Council reviewed and commented on the
draft RFP. The City Council then authorized the City Manager to proceed with issuing
the RFP. City staff released the RFP for consideration and received two proposals. Staff
has reviewed the proposals, interviewed the consultants and is recommending that the
Council award a contract to MIG lnc.

REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL:

After City Council review of the RFP, the City Manager directed the Community and
Economic Development Department to release the RFP for consideration by
professional planning firms. The Planning Division circulated the RFP to 10 planning
firms including AECOM, City Place Planning, ESA, Gruen Associates, Michael Baker
lnternational, MIG lnc., Place Works, Raimi Associates, Rangwala Associates and T&B
Planning. To ensure that the consultants understood the scope of the project, the RFP
included a pre-submittal meeting. The pre-submittal meeting was conducted on the
afternoon of January 10, 2019. Both MIG lnc., and Michael Baker lnternational were
present at the pre-submittal meeting along with a few of their sub-consultants.

The RFP was circulated for a period of 39 days starting on December 21,2018 with
proposal due to the City no later than January 28,2019 at 4:30 p.m. RFPs such as this
are usually circulated for a 30 day period, but an additional nine days was provided
since the RFP went out during the holiday season. This allowed consultants adequate
time to submit proposal to the City. On January 28, 2019, the City received two
proposals, one from MIG lnc., and the other Michael Baker lnternational.

After receiving the proposals, a rating panel was established to review and rate each
proposal. The rating panel included the Director of Planning and Community
Development, Michael Huntley, the Senior Planner, Samantha Tewasart and the Deputy
Director of Public Works, Frank Lopez. Each of the proposals was ranked based on the
criteria provided in the RFP and included interviews with each of the consulting teams.

Each of the two firms and their respective sub-consultants are very qualified and quite
capable of completing this project. Both firms have done works for the City including
work on the existing General Plan elements and environmental work for some of the
major projects. However, it is the panel's determination that MIG scored slightly higher
on the first two categories below and higher on the last category:

  O  Qualifications of the consulting team and sub consultants on similar projects;

  a  lnnovation and ability to update a General Plan addressing changes in
  technology and development trends; and

  a  Overall proposed budget for the project.

Although the City Council made it clear that the budget was not the determining factor,
but the quality of the consulting firm and their ability to prepare a quality product, it is still
one of the factors in the decision as well. As it relates to MIG lnc., its proposed budget
for the project is $681,461, and Michael Baker lnternational proposed budget is
$961,000. Although both bids may seem high, staff conducted a survey before we
started this process to determine what the approximate cost was to prepare a General
Plan update. Of the nine cities surveyed, the cost for such a project ranged from as low

necessary to facilitate the project. Since staff is recommending MIG lnc., there is a

update project.

 A Dynamic City
Monterey Park is a dynamic community,
having experienced ebbs and flows of
development and demographic change,
since its founding in 1916. During its first
two decades of cityhood, the community
grew slowly, as new Asian immigrants
established farms in the area, contributing
to the diversity of residents that included
descendants of Mexican ranchers and settlers
from the Midwest. Real estate developers
looked to create subdivisions rivaling those
in Beverly Hills and Bel Air. Their investments
are evident today in the Cascades fountain.
While the Great Depression dampened
these efforts, by the end of World War II,
the City experienced explosive growth as
new suburban housing tracts sprung up to
accommodate the many veterans and their
new families.

EnCodePlus to provide the latest in land use and scenario modeling, interactive online engagement,
and interactive zoning ordinances to the planning process.

We believe in a planning process that engages the whole community, is visionary and innovative,
addresses placemaking and enhances the urban fabric of Monterey Park, and challenges
conventional wisdom through incorporating new ideas and creating unique places. The Michael
Baker Team draws upon the depth and breadth of an inter-disciplinary bench of planners, scientists,
historians, and urban designers, and engineers to bring multiple viewpoints to policy and program
topics. We can respond to any issue that may arise during the planning process!

 • Urban Design Studio. Our interdisciplinary studio is accomplished in developing place
  and improving upon a community’s strength and existing fabric. We will use our placemaking
  capabilities to help plan for land uses that are demanded by modern workforces, restoring
  the context of community as championed by re-urban pioneers such as the venerable Jane
  Jacobs, Duany & Plater-Zyberk, and Peter Calthorpe. Michael Baker recently completed the
  South Garfield Village Specific Plan and design for South Garfield that incorporated the City’s
  first pedestrian hybrid beacon at a mid-block crossing and low-impact design stormwater
  treatment and retention. We are currently involved in multiple active transportation projects

  SUBJEGT:  Appoint members to the General Plan Advisory Committee

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Appointing members to the General Plan Advisory Committee;
  2. Appointing five alternates: and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

The City Council authorized staff to proceed with circulating a Request for Proposal
(RFP) to solicit proposals from professional planning firms to assist the City with the
preparation of an update to the City's General Plan. Proposals were submitted to the
City and reviewed by an internal review committee. Once the City Council awards the
contract, it is staff's intent to meet with the General Plan Advisory Committee (GPAC) to
begin the General Plan update process. lt is therefore important to appoint the GPAC
members so that staff can conduct an orientation and begin the General Plan update
process.

BACKGROUND:

The City's last comprehensive General Plan update occurred in 2001. As part of the
General Plan update process at that time, the City Council established a GPAC and
appointed members from the community to assist City staff and consulting team. The
establishment of an ad-hoc committee is not an uncommon practice since community
outreach and feedback are key components to ensure the development of a community
based comprehensive long-range plan.

At the City Council meeting on December 20, 2018, staff provided the City Council an
opportunity to review the draft Request for Proposal (RFP) soliciting professional
planning services to update the General Plan. The RFP included a section that identifies
the establishment of the GPAC. The City Council did provide general comments on the
GPAC.

  Page 577 of 579
 Staff Report - General Plan Advisory Committee

It is now time for the City Council to consider appointments to GPAC. The GPAC is an
ad-hoc committee with a total of eleven members. Each Council member will appoint
two members each, and the City Manager will appoint the eleventh member. Statf is
also requesting that each Council member appoint one alternate to the committee as
well just in case one of the members decides not to participate. This will allow the
GPAC to proceed without having to return to the City Council to seek another
appointment.

To facilitate in the establishment of the GPAC, staff reached out to the community
seeking interested individuals who wish to participate in the General Plan update
process. Below is a list of individuals who are interested in participating and who the
City Council may wish to consider. The list is not exclusive and Councilmembers may,
of course, select someone other than those on the list. However, staff would suggest
that those other potential committee members have some understanding of planning,
land use, environmental, development, real estate, public administration or public sector
financial experience.
